newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - US economy makes Clinton shoo-in - Nomura.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - US economy makes Clinton shoo-in - Nomura.

text.p: Echoing the 1992 U.S. presidential campaign's motto "It's the economy, stupid," an economic analysis by Nomura Securities International found President Bill Clinton is a shoo-in for reelection.
"Economics is about all you need to know to determine who is going to win the elections," Nomura Securities International chief economist David Resler told Reuters on Monday.

"The analysis of economic factors point to two important conclusions. One is that incumbents do well when the economy does well, which means it is likely President Clinton will remain president," Resler also said.

"But it's likely the control of Congress will be retained by the Republicans. That's what the economic analysis tells us," added Resler who expected the U.S. Treasury market to prefer such balance of powers.

"If we end up with a Democratic control of both houses and the White House, bond yields will be higher not because of the policy that will emerge, but because of the perception of the bond market there will not be the balancing forces that we would have had with split control," Resler also said.
Resler expected the Republicans, if they retain control of Congress, to be more willing to compromise.

"Since 1952, it has always correctly predicted the winner," Resler found. "Ask: 'Is the incumbent running for reelection? Has there been a recession in the last 24 months?' If the answer to that last question is 'No,' the incumbent wins."
However, Resler also noted "economic variables don't explain the voting success of an incumbent on a state-by-state basis."
"Economic success rewards incumbent presidents. But, generally, economic success rewards incumbents," Resler noted.
Such finding may account for the Republicans retaining control of the House.
Resler found no evidence "there is any impact at all of economic variables on the Senate elections."
The bad news for Clinton is the turn-out is typically low when the economy does well -- including among those most likely to vote for him.

"In a feel-good economy, people act on the 'if it's not broken, don't fix it' principle," said Resler who drew this conclusion based on past performance of the Conference Board's consumer confidence index and voters' turn-out.
He predicted voters' turn-out in November will be 2.5 percentage points lower than in 1992.
Worse of all for the president, Resler's analysis implied that only one in 10 people who found a job during the Clinton administration are likely to vote at all.
Opinions poll show Clinton leading Dole by a comfortable margin.
